content: Performance indicator analysis and the development of action plans based on the results are essential to optimize HIV treatment and reduce the emergence of HIV drug resistance (HIV-DR). The WHO Consolidated Guidelines on the Use of Antiretroviral Drugs for Treating and Preventing HIV Infection emphasize the importance of routine monitoring of early warning indicators (EWIs) and periodic surveys in specific populations. These surveys are critical for informing the selection of antiretroviral regimens and determining the frequency of viral load monitoring. Such activities should be integrated into national HIV strategic plans. Surveys should target specific groups, such as individuals recently infected with HIV (to document and characterize the transmission of drug-resistant virus) and infants under 18 months of age (to guide the selection of first-line regimens for children). The WHO recommends prioritizing surveys on pre-treatment drug resistance (PDR) and acquired drug resistance (ADR), with PDR assessments conducted every three years (e.g., in years 1, 4, and 7) and ADR assessments in years 2, 5, and 8. Alternatively, these surveys can be combined and conducted simultaneously. Countries should determine the optimal sequencing of these surveys based on the type of epidemic and the status and coverage of their national antiretroviral therapy (ART) programs. HIV-DR data should be made available to support national decision-making, particularly when updating adult and pediatric ART guidelines. The guidelines will be updated every three years, either fully or partially, based on changes in evidence or user needs. Technical updates on specific subjects may also be produced as necessary. Dissemination will occur through print publications, electronic formats on the WHO website, and supplementary materials containing supporting documentation and evidence. Selected systematic reviews and evidence will also be published in peer-reviewed journals to support dissemination. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices, as well as implementing partners, to ensure effective communication and adaptation of the guidelines through regional and subregional meetings. Countries are encouraged to analyze the budgetary, human resource, and health system implications of implementing these guidelines to identify available resources and areas requiring additional investment. Broad stakeholder engagement in policy design, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) will help ensure that national adaptations of the guidelines result in HIV programs that are legitimate, acceptable, effective, equitable, and responsive to community needs. National HIV programs should identify a package of high-impact interventions covering the full continuum of HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care services. This package should be included in the national health benefit package and funded, at least partially, through the national health financing system. The package must be adapted for different populations, locations, and settings and regularly reviewed and updated as necessary. Recognizing that it may not be feasible to fund and implement the full range of interventions immediately, a phased approach should be adopted, progressively expanding the range of services offered and the populations covered while reducing out-of-pocket expenses for users. The recommendations in these guidelines should be considered within the broader context of national health benefit packages and the full range of HIV interventions and services. Where dedicated national HIV budgets exist, prioritization of HIV interventions will be necessary. In the absence of such budgets, the prioritization of HIV interventions must be considered alongside other essential health interventions. Clear criteria should be established to guide prioritization within the range of HIV interventions and services and across the broader national health benefit package. Implementation tools will be published alongside the guidelines, including resources for costing, planning, and country case studies. The ultimate goal of implementing these recommendations is to achieve and sustain universal coverage of services to maximize the impact on the HIV epidemic. Countries are encouraged to set ambitious targets and make every effort to achieve them. However, disparities in service coverage, capacity limitations, resource constraints, and quality concerns may necessitate a phased or sequenced approach to implementing new recommendations. Cost estimation is a critical step in the rollout process. Several costing tools and resources are available to assist countries in estimating costs and budgeting for HIV-related interventions and services. For example, the Spectrum suite of models includes tools such as the AIDS Impact Model (AIM) and the Goals module, which can estimate the impact of new recommendations on AIDS-related mortality, infant infections, treatment needs, and costs. The OneHealth tool is another resource designed to strengthen health system analysis, costing, and financing scenario development at the country level. Both Spectrum and OneHealth are available for free download. WHO and collaborating organizations have also developed tools to assist with drug quantification and supply management. These tools are available for download and include descriptions of their main purposes and programmatic focus. Additionally, a flexible tool for costing investments in critical enablers, such as integrated treatment and rights literacy programs, stigma and discrimination reduction programs, and training for healthcare workers, has been developed and is freely available. Evaluation of the guidelines will be conducted to assess their uptake into national policies and programs. Data will be made available through the WHO country intelligence database, which is updated every six months to reflect changes in policy and implementation across lowand middle-income countries and selected high-income countries.
